raw_response:
I am 73 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man. My bones know this soil better than any book. I have six mu of good land, and I will not gamble with it at my age. In Quzhou, the land rewards those who stick to what works: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is what I have always done, and that is what I will do this year.

My wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. I used an improved Jimai variety — not the fanciest seed, but it stands up to the dry winds here and does not lodging easily. I will irrigate it three times: once when it greens up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The groundwater is not what it used to be, so I will not waste water. I will put down about 16 jin of nitrogen fertilizer per mu, split between the green-up and jointing stages, plus some phosphorus and potassium as base dressing. Two sprays should keep the weeds and diseases in check — I have seen too many young farmers spray five or six times for nothing.

After the wheat comes off in early June, I will not waste a single day. I will rotary-till the stubble and plant hybrid maize the same week. Summer maize needs every day of sunshine it can get. I will irrigate it twice — at the big flare stage and at filling — and fertilize much like the wheat. Hybrid seed costs more, but it pays back in the yield.

I have thought about cotton or vegetables, but at my age, with only primary schooling, I do not have the strength or the market connections for those risky crops. Wheat and maize feed my family, and the government buys them at a fair price. That is security. I plough before wheat and rotary-till before maize, just as my father did, just as I have always done.
